The Simple Past and The Past Continuous Tenses
When you talk about events in your life, it is common to use a mixture of tenses. This allows you to convey a variety of timelines and action sequences.

You use the Simple Past tense to talk about many kinds of past events: short, quickly finished actions, longer situations and repeated events.
  • I did a lot of work.
  • They hired me right away.
  • I needed to find a quick fix to the problem.

You use the Past Continuous tense to talk about an event that was happening at a time before now.
  • I was interviewing in the city.
  • I was getting anxious.
  • I was starting to get frustrated.

When you want to learn more about a company, you can talk to a professional to get more information. The kinds of questions you ask the professional will serve as clues for them to know what kind of information and/or answer you are looking for.

You can ask for:
  • background information
  • reasons
  • examples
  • ideas
  • suggestions
  • opinions


Remember that when asking for information you can Wh- words.

images.text:
Kristi: Ms. Elison? Do you have a minute?
Janet: Kristi, yes. Come in. Have a seat. What's on your mind?
Kristi: You mentioned that you started Polygon as a start up company. How did you get your start in the PR industry?
Janet: I did a lot of non-profit work, during which I happened to do PR but I didn't know what it was called. I liked doing it, and it was always what I gravitated toward.

Kristi: Why did you decide to become an entrepreneur?
Janet: When I was finishing up grad school, I was interviewing in Chicago. I was hired by a company to do their communications and marketing. While I was working there, I started to get referrals, which is why I opened up my own firm.
Kristi: What challenges did you face owning your own PR firm?
Janet: The referrals turned from B2B to more beauty and lifestyle; there isn't much monetary business there so I had to find clients that were going to provide more financial stability.

Kristi: How did you feel about that?
Janet: I mean I could ask for whatever amount of money I wanted when the clients came to me, but when you're pitching clients, it's a competitive situation and you have to cut your rates which isn't good financially. So, if I was going to continue to run my firm, I needed to raise capital.
Kristi: What else besides capital are necessary tools to create a firm and sustain it?
Janet: It's a given that you have to have talent. Also, do you have your niche covered? Do you know the kind of media that your client is looking for? Do you have clients that need publicity, or another type of PR, such as crisis management? You need to know your strengths.
